svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the AWS Config seventy-seven new resource types announcement changes, depending on which recording strategy an account uses. AWS states that AWS Config now supports seventy-seven additional AWS resource types across key services including Amazon EC2, Amazon S3 Files and Amazon Q Business, that with this launch if you have enabled recording for all resource types then AWS Config will automatically track these new additions, that the newly supported resource types are also available in Config rules and Config aggregators, and that they can be monitored in all AWS Regions where the resources are available. The consequence splits by strategy. An account recording all resource types gains the coverage with no action taken and gains the configuration item volume with it, so the bill moves without a change on the account's side and the only way to decline is to change the recording strategy itself. An account recording a selected list of types gains nothing and will gain nothing until the list is edited, which is the trade that was made when the list was chosen and the reason a selected list needs revisiting on a cadence rather than only at setup. The cost model is recorded from a worked example on the AWS Config pricing page, since the rate tables themselves are rendered client-side and carry no figures in the served page: three tenths of a cent per continuous configuration item, one point two cents per periodic configuration item, and under periodic recording only one configuration item per resource is generated per day. Dividing the periodic rate by the continuous rate gives four, so a resource changing more than four times a day is cheaper recorded continuously and a resource changing less often is cheaper recorded periodically, which makes recording frequency a per-resource-type decision rather than an account-wide one, and most of the newly added types are the static kind. Config rules are charged separately per rule evaluation per region, in tiers of the first hundred thousand evaluations, the next four hundred thousand, and five hundred thousand and one or more, with the rate per tier deliberately not quoted because the page does not serve it, so a rule scoped to all supported resource types now has more resources to evaluate and that is a second cost line moving for the same reason as the first, which can also move a compliance count without any resource being misconfigured. Several of the new types are controls rather than workloads, including GuardDuty threat and trusted entity sets, an Inspector version two code security scan configuration, a Braket spending limit and a Bedrock AgentCore payment connector, and for a control it is the modification that is the security event, so configuration history makes a quiet narrowing of a detector into a diffable record. The operational note is that none of this produces an alert: the coverage improves silently, the volume increases silently, and the first visible signal is a bill or a Config rule reporting on resources nobody had scoped it to.
svg.title: Seventy-seven types, and only one kind of account has to act
svg.text: The coverage widened for free. The volume widened with it.
AWS Config — 77 new resource types, “in all AWS Regions where the resources are available”.
The sentence to read twice
“if you have enabled recording for all resource types, then AWS Config will automatically track these new additions”
Recording ALL types
→ coverage gained, no action taken
→ CI volume gained with it
→ the bill moves on AWS’s schedule
Nothing to do but notice. Declining means changing
the strategy, not the launch.
The contract working exactly as written.
Recording a SELECTED list
→ nothing changed
→ 77 types supported and unrecorded
→ until somebody edits the list
The control working, and the blind spot growing.
A list needs a review date, not just a setup date.
Its failure mode is staying correct while the world widens.
Two rates, four times apart — and a ceiling on one of them
$0.003 per continuous configuration item (worked example)
$0.012 per periodic configuration item (worked example)
“Under periodic recording, only 1 configuration item per resource is generated per day”
0.012 / 0.003 = 4 changes/day — above it continuous wins, below it periodic does
Most of these 77 are the static kind. So frequency is a per-type decision, and this is the moment to make it.
The second line, easy to miss
Rules bill “per rule evaluation per region”, tiered.
A rule scoped to ALL_SUPPORTED now has more to
evaluate — and newly supported resources are
usually untagged, so a count moves.
Several of the 77 are controls, not workloads
GuardDuty::TrustedEntitySet · ThreatEntitySet
InspectorV2::CodeSecurityScanConfiguration
Braket::SpendingLimit · LicenseManager::Grant
For a control, the modification is the security event.
None of it produces an alert
Coverage improved silently. Volume increased silently. The first visible signal is a bill — or a Config rule
reporting findings on resources nobody scoped it to, which looks like a regression and is a wider population.
A compliance percentage can fall because the denominator grew. Same week, third time.
“in all AWS Regions where the resources are available” is a conditional, and the condition is per type.
